items.abstract: <jats:p>Multi-agent reinforcement learning is increasingly used to coordinate storage, on-site generation, and flexible loads in grid-interactive building clusters. However, most evidence is reported for a single district size, and electricity cost is often treated as a proxy for operational carbon. This study benchmarks a rule-based controller, centralised soft actor-critic, independent per-building soft actor-critic, and multi-agent reinforcement learning with iterative sequential action selection (MARLISA) while sweeping cluster size from 1 to 17 buildings in the CityLearn 2022 benchmark. Each configuration uses three random seeds and a fixed 30-episode training budget; thermal comfort transfer is assessed on the six-building CityLearn 2023 dynamics-enabled dataset. The results distinguish two forms of scalability. Centralised control has an almost size-independent wall-clock cost per episode, whereas decentralised controllers scale approximately linearly because they instantiate one agent per building. Control quality shows the opposite pattern: centralised performance deteriorates as the cluster grows, while per-building agents remain comparatively stable and outperform centralised control beyond two buildings. Doubling the training budget at 17 buildings does not recover centralised performance, indicating a capacity limitation rather than only under-training. MARLISA provides no measurable benefit over independent agents under default hyperparameters. All learning controllers reduce cost and operational carbon relative to the uncontrolled baseline, but carbon reductions consistently lag cost reductions. On the dynamics-enabled dataset, energy gains coexist with persistent thermal-comfort violations because the storage-oriented reward omits temperature. Coordination architecture should therefore be selected against the binding computational or learning constraint, while carbon and comfort must be represented explicitly in the control objective.</jats:p>
